name: Revolut
summary: Revolut's interviews are commonly described as fast-moving and demanding, with a strong focus on ownership, structured problem-solving and measurable results. Candidates usually report an early recruiter call and, for many roles, an online test or task, then interviews on their skills and a problem-solving case. Engineering candidates typically discuss coding and system design, and the exact stages vary by team.
rounds: Recruiter or introductory call on your background and motivation
Online test or take-home task for many roles
Skills interview with the team on your experience and technical or functional depth
Problem-solving or case interview, often with numbers and a recommendation
Final interview with a senior team member for some roles
looks_for: Ownership: driving work to a result without waiting to be told
Speed with quality: moving quickly without cutting corners on risk or customers
Structured problem-solving and comfort with numbers
High standards and a habit of pushing for a better result
For risk, fraud and compliance roles: sound judgement on financial crime and regulation

questions.text: Tell me about the achievement you're proudest of. What exactly did you do, and how did you measure it?
covers: Your own part, separated clearly from the team's
The metric that moved and by how much
Why it mattered to the customer or the business

questions.text: Tell me about a time you delivered something much faster than people expected.
covers: The usual timeline and why it was too slow
What you cut, automated or did in parallel
What you did to keep quality and risk under control

questions.text: Tell me about a time you refused to settle for 'good enough' and pushed for a better result.
covers: What 'good enough' looked like and why it fell short
How you raised the bar and brought others with you
The better result, with a number

questions.text: Describe a time you dug into data to find the root cause of a problem everyone else had explained away.
covers: The accepted explanation and why you doubted it
The data you went through yourself
The root cause, the fix and the effect

questions.text: Tell me about a time you failed at something important. What did you change afterwards?
covers: A real failure, owned in the first person
What you'd do differently, specifically
Evidence that the change has worked since

questions.text: How would you design a system that stops card fraud in real time without blocking too many good customers?
covers: Signals: amount, merchant, device, location and the customer's usual behaviour
Scoring within the payment's time limit, with rules and a model
Options beyond decline, such as an in-app confirmation, and learning from outcomes

questions.text: A customer says money left their account for a payment they didn't make. Walk me through how you'd handle it.
covers: Protecting the account first: freezing the card and checking the customer's identity
Working out what happened: card misuse, a scam where they were tricked, or a merchant error
Explaining the next steps and timelines honestly, and recording the case

questions.text: How would you make sure a money transfer is never processed twice, even if the app retries the request?
covers: An idempotency key sent with the request and stored with the result
An atomic check, such as a unique constraint, so two requests can't both win
Timeouts, retries from other systems and a reconciliation to catch anything missed

questions.text: How would you estimate how many people in Bengaluru might use a multi-currency travel card in a year?
covers: Starting from the adult population and the share who travel abroad
Assumptions for how many would use a card for it, and how often
A sanity check and the assumption that matters most

questions.text: Which metrics would you track for a new savings feature in a banking app, and what would make you change course?
covers: One main metric, such as active savers or money saved
Guardrails: support contacts, complaints and customers leaving
The result, decided in advance, that would make you change or stop it

questions.text: What is transaction monitoring, and how would you cut false alerts without missing true cases of money laundering?
covers: Rules and models that flag unusual patterns for review
Tuning thresholds by customer type and risk, using past alert outcomes
Testing any change before release and documenting it for regulators

questions.text: Why Revolut, and which part of the product would you most like to work on?
covers: A specific product or team, not just the brand
What you'd bring to it from your experience
Why a fast-growing financial company suits you

questions.text: Which Revolut feature would you improve, and how would you know your change worked?
covers: A specific feature and a real customer problem with it
The change you'd make and what you'd leave out
The metric that would show it helped

questions.text: This role moves fast and asks a lot. Why does that kind of environment suit you?
covers: An example of you doing well under pace and pressure
How you keep quality up when moving quickly
What you want to learn from it

tips: Bring numbers to every story: what changed, by how much and how quickly.
Practise a structured case answer out loud: clarify the goal, break the problem down, estimate, then recommend.
Use the app or read about its features, and come with one specific, realistic idea for improving a part of it.
For engineering roles, practise explaining payments trade-offs: consistency, retries, idempotency and audit trails.
Expect pushback on your answers; defend your reasoning calmly, and change your view if you're given a better fact.
The stages vary by team, so ask the recruiter what each interview will cover and prepare for that.
